speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: EXCHANGE OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH U.S. RESPECTING BALANCE OF PAYMENTS
speechtext:
should like to table copies of letters which were exchanged yesterday between the secretary of the United States treasury, Hon. Henry H. Fowler, and myself.
These letters review the unique financial relationship between Canada and the United States and the continuing exemption for Canada from the balance of payments programs of the United States. They repeat the judgment of both governments that a continued improvement in the international payments position of the United States is important for Canada and for the international monetary system as well as for the United States. They confirm the assurances of the Canadian government that Canada's exemption from the United States balance of payments programs will not be used in such a way as to endanger the success of those programs. In particular I have reiterated that it is not an objective of Canadian policy to achieve permanent increases in our exchange reserves through unnecessary borrowing in the United States.
At the same time the secretary of the United States treasury and 1 have agreed that the implementation of this principle does not require that Canada's reserve level be limited to any particular figure, and that our reserves may be expected to fluctuate to accommodate the adaptation of monetary policy to the changing needs of our domestic economy, seasonal influences, and other influences of a temporary nature.
I propose, Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house that the texts of these letters be appended to Hansard.

think it would add anything to the situation simply to say that both countries believe it is in their interest to occasion destabilizing influences on their respective currencies which might inhibit the other country in the pursuit of its own economic objectives.
I note the very general terms in which the minister has indicated that the $2.55 billion, which he calls a target figure and which has long been recognized as the ceiling, is now subject to temporary deviation. As a matter of fact it may be that for all practical purposes it has gone. If this is the true result then I would say it is a step in the right direction. For over a year now I have been saying that this restriction has been strangling us in Canada. Indeed, I would say to the minister it is very fortunate that Canada has been able to obtain this relaxation, though why a ceiling was ever imposed is something one will always question.
As I say, it is fortunate that Canada is not now caught by this limit, because before long the hon. gentleman would have been obliged to go into the market to raise funds had this ceiling not been removed. After all, we know that long term interest rates are now at the highest point ever. Last week the average rate on government long term obligations was up to 7.16, and this would have occasioned an increased movement of foreign funds into Canada.

The result would have been that the Minister of Finance, through the Bank of Canada, would have had to go into the market to sweep up these excess foreign funds, particularly United States funds, in order to limit our holdings to the $2.55 billion figure. I trust the government will now have a more effective tool in dealing with the problem of inflation. As a matter of fact we are still facing that problem, but this might be allowing the government a bit more room for manoeuvre. We have not yet got rid of all the shackles that the action back in 1963 and 1964 brought on, but I am glad to see that after a

subtopic: ANTI-DUMPING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for Canada one of the important elements of the Kennedy round package was the new international code to govern the application of anti-dumping duties. Canadian representatives took an active part in negotiating the code to ensure that it would enable the application of dumping duties quickly and effectively when dumping caused or threatened injury to Canadian industry and, at the same time, protect Canadian exporters against the unreasonable use of these measures by other countries. Other signatories to the code have been complying with its provisions since July 1, 1968, as agreed at the end of the Kennedy round. It was not possible for Canada to meet that date and it was agreed with our trading partners that Canada could delay its implementation until January 1 next.
As hon. members are aware, new legislation is required for Canada to give effect to the code. It will be recalled that the white paper on anti-dumping, which was tabled in the house on September 20, incorporated a draft anti-dumping act designed to comply with the provisions of the anti-dumping code. This white paper has been subjected to a detailed examination by the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs which held twenty two meetings for this purpose. In the course of this study, the committee heard extensive evidence from industry representatives and government officials. This evidence forms part of the printed proceedings which have been available for some days.
The report of the committee recommends the draft bill and the white paper to this house for favourable consideration together

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
with the changes set forth in this report. These recommendations have been incorporated into the present bill, to be based on this resolution. I should like to note the way in which members of all parties worked together on the finance committee in studying this important measure. I should certainly like to congratulate the members of the committee and its chairman, the member for Gatineau on the effort they put forward, enabling them to make a report to the house on their studies so expeditiously.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on the principal features of the proposed legislation. The bill relates to the imposition of anti-dumping duties including provisional duties, the establishment of an anti-dumping tribunal and certain consequential amendments to the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff and the Tariff Board Act.
Under the terms of this bill goods are considered to be dumped if the normal value exceeds the export price and the dumping duty applicable or the margin of dumping is the difference between these two amounts. Normal value is generally the price at which like goods are sold at arms length in the ordinary course of trade in the country of export at about the same time as the goods are sold to the Canadian importer, adjusted for allowances to reflect price comparability between the home market sales and the sale to the Canadian importer.
Export price is defined as an amount equal to the lesser of the exporter's sale price for the goods or the importer's purchase price for the goods on an f.o.b. basis. If the dumped goods cause injury, threat of injury or material retardation to production in Canada, dumping duties will be applied.
The Department of National Revenue is to retain responsibility for deciding whether or not goods are dumped into Canada. It will also be responsible for making preliminary determinations of dumping and the consequent levying of provisional duties. These duties would be collected after a preliminary determination by the deputy minister and would apply to all imports of such goods until there is an order or finding by the tribunal. After an order or finding the deputy minister makes a final determination and definitive duties are applied to all subsequent importations of like goods that are dumped. National Revenue's decision on the margin of dumping and the category of goods involved will be subject to appeal to the Tariff Board and, on points of law, to the Exchequer Court. These

appeal provisions are analogous to the appeal provisions set out in the Customs Act.
The most significant change required in Canadian legislation relates to the provision that there must be a formal inquiry into the impact of dumping on production in Canada. This requirement is carried forward from the anti-dumping code which provides that injury, threat of injury or material retardation to production in Canada must be determined before dumping duties are assessed. An anti-dumping tribunal to be composed of not more than five members is to be established for this purpose. The tribunal must, within three months from the date of the deputy minister's preliminary determination, make a decision on the question of injury, threat of injury or material retardation to production in Canada. If the tribunal makes an order or finding of injury, the deputy minister of national revenue must make a final determination as to the margin of dumping.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
A number of enforcement provisions have been built into the proposed act to enable the Department of National Revenue and the tribunal to obtain the necessary data and arrive at decisions within the framework of the time limits provided for in the bill. Accordingly it will not be possible for importers to escape anti-dumping duties by either supplying incorrect information or withholding information. On the other hand, importers and exporters who conduct their affairs in a legitimate manner have nothing to fear from the most vigorous application of these provisions.
In so far as the consequential amendments are concerned, the only substantive revision relates to the proposed deletion of subsection 7 of section 40A of the Customs Act. This section provides for the establishment of arbitrary or fixed valuations in respect of goods which are sold to importers in Canada at prices similar to those prevailing in the country of export and therefore are not dumped but are judged to be causing injury to Canadian producers. We are proposing that this section be replaced by a new provision which will achieve the same result as the present law through the use of a surtax rather than anti-dumping duties. Emergency action of this kind is contemplated under Article XIX of the GATT.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to state, and I am stating, that in the government's view the proposed legislation reflects

the needs of the Canadian economy in this post-Kennedy round period by providing a comprehensive framework within which action can be taken swiftly to counteract dumping that is injurious to Canadian producers. subtopic: ANTI-DUMPING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the season of the year and the circumstances which exist at the present time in this house there is no intention on the part of this party of prolonging debate on this legislation. Perhaps even more important than that is the fact which was mentioned by the parliamentary secretary that the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs had a long series of meetings on this legislation at which we heard explanations from officials of the Department of Finance and of the Department of National Revenue, and briefs from groups representing most of the major industries in Canada, particularly all those which are likely to be especially affected by this legislation.
Dumping, Mr. Chairman, has been a problem throughout the history of our country. It can, does and will continue to cause serious injury to Canadian industry when it occurs. Dumping, or the sale of goods in Canada at a lower price than those goods are sold at in the country of export and which thereby causes injury to Canadian industry, in that simple form is very easy to define. However, the discovery of when dumping is actually taking place and the taking of effective measures to prevent it are very different matters.
The matter of determining when dumping is taking place was brought to our attention by a lot of the evidence supplied by Canadian industries that we heard in the standing committee. We also had a lot of evidence about past failure to take action after dumping had been brought to the attention of the Department of National Revenue. One of the great difficulties is that if dumping takes place it can cause serious injury to Canadian industry before it is detected. Even though the amount of dumping may not be massive, even though it may be relatively small, the entry of goods at dump prices can lower the entire market, thus putting Canadian industries into a loss position and in some cases
Ways and Means
forcing them to close down with a consequent loss of jobs, a loss of taxes to the dominion government, and so on. Therefore dumping is an extremely serious matter.
We also were given evidence in the committee that devices of many kinds are employed to conceal the fact that dumping is taking place or has taken place. In fact I think a statement was made by one of the witnesses to the effect that a manufacturer in a foreign country and an importer in Canada who knew all the ropes were in a position to evade completely our dumping laws. I would hope that the administration of this new dumping legislation which we are in process of passing will put an end to statements of that kind, which were not challenged by the officials of the departments represented at the hearings. In other words, I hope that this sort of thing will not continue.
The emphasis in most of the briefs presented by industries that were represented at the committee hearings was to the effect that improved administrative practices and greater speed are necessary to ensure that dumping does not take place, and that these are essential if this new legislation is to be effective. I would like to put on the record two statements made by industries, which are typical of the type of statements we heard in the committee. The first is to be found at page 966 of the evidence and reads as follows:
In conclusion-
That is, in concluding their brief.
-we consider the draft Canadian anti-dumping act provides the broad discretionary powers necessary to permit the authorities to apply this instrument effectively. However, its effectiveness will depend largely upon the spirit and manner in which it is administered and the calibre of the people involved.
Therefore, we consider it is of the utmost importance that the officials responsible for its administration should not only be fully qualified to properly discharge their duties, but should also be fully aware of the need to function expeditiously, aggressively and with Canada's best interest in mind.
This sort of statement was repeated in brief after brief. I think there is no question that the effectiveness of this new legislation will depend almost entirely on how well it is administered. I have hope that the administration will be improved, and later I will touch on one or two points in that connection.
I think the statement I have just quoted indicates pretty fairly the general consensus of the views of industry in regard to the legislation when it says that the draft antidumping act provides the broad discretionary

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
powers necessary to enable effective antidumping measures to be taken. Therefore once more it comes down to the matter of administration.
I wish to quote briefly from one other brief, again under the heading of administration. It reads:
Before this new code goes into effect, the customs division should become so organized that it can proceed thoroughly and quickly, and should have the will to do so.
If the new code is to be applied "quickly and effectively", there is need for:
1.	More information on entries.
2.	More prompt reporting of entries by local ports of entry.
3.	More information relating to imports, which should be made available to the central administrative authorities more quickly.
4.	Improved mechanism for the determination of values abroad.
5.	Improved government facilities to establish facts promptly, which have been notably inadequate in the past, even when there were acceptable home market sales in an exporting country for like products.
The administrative machinery of the Department of National Revenue should be overhauled to ensure the prompt availability of all data, whether it is to be obtained from abroad or from records in Canada.
I think we cannot overemphasize the importance of improved administration and great speed in detecting dumping and in taking the proper measures to put an end to it.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Some of the evidence we were given was to the effect that more Department of National Revenue officers are required overseas to investigate the prices at which goods are being sold in various countries so that individual complaints made by Canadian producers that dumping is taking place may be investigated. The officials of the two departments who were present stated that plans were under way for an increase in the number of officials abroad. I hope the government will take action along this line in spite of the austerity program which they have been talking about to such an extent and in spite of the freeze on the size of the civil service.
One thing which I believe is absolutely essential is that Canadian industry be protected against dumping. This is essential in order to ensure that employment continues at a reasonable level and also that there is a tax base upon which the government can obtain sufficient funds to carry on all the varied activities in which the government is now engaged. Therefore this is a case in respect of

which I would hope the present freeze on increasing the number of civil servants will not apply so that a sufficient number of officers of the Department of National Revenue may be sent to overseas posts in order that proper information can be collected with which to properly administer the act.
The parliamentary secretary noted the fact that the committee recognized a considerable number of changes should be made to the draft bill contained in the white paper which was put before the committee. I believe the effect of these recommended changes will be to very greatly improve the bill. I was, therefore, happy to hear the parliamentary secretary state that these changes are being incorporated. I take it that they are incorporated or will be incorporated in full in the bill that will be produced as soon as the resolution stage is completed. I can assure him and members of the house that that in itself will of course greatly expedite the passage of the bill through the house.
I shall not refer in detail to the recommended changes, but I should like to note one of the most important. I refer to the elimination of section 30 in the draft bill which provided for a panel of deputy ministers whose view had to be secured before the tribunal set up to determine if dumping had taken place could take any action at all. I think it was quite apparent to quite a number of members of the committee and the representatives of practically every industry which mentioned the matter that this panel of deputy ministers was an unnecessary step in the procedure and one which was bound to cause delay. Therefore I am delighted that it has been eliminated. It seems to be a very peculiar sort of organization to deal with this whole matter in any event.
There is one other matter about which I should like to speak and which was referred to by the parliamentary secretary. It concerns the elimination of section 7 of the Customs Act and the substitution of section 37 as it was in the draft bill. I do not know what the number will be in the bill to be introduced until we actually receive it. The main point is that a great deal of damage can be done to Canadian industry by importations which are not dumping under the definition of that term but are importations at a fairly or very low price. This type of importation takes place at the end of a season, at the end of a run or because of something else along that line. It happens when the product is being sold in the country of manufacture or production at a
December 17, 1268

price lower than the price which has prevailed previously or which normally prevails. Or it may be that because of certain particular circumstances the product is being produced at an abnormally low price. Importations of this kind have caused more damage and have been more difficult to deal with than ordinary dumping.
One of the best examples of this type of importation is in the fruit and vegetable industry. Our position north of the United States has made us particularly vulnerable in this regard. There is the situation in respect of strawberries. The strawberry season in the United States begins some four or five weeks before the season begins in Canada. By the time the strawberry harvest has begun in Canada it is about at an end in the United States. The cream has been taken off the market, so to speak, and the price has dropped to very low levels in the United States. When the strawberries are imported into Canada at that price, although it is the price at which they are sold in the United States it means that the Canadian industry cannot operate properly. Other fruits and vegetables are affected to a greater or less extent in the same way. Thus, in order to enable Canada to maintain a healthy fruit and vegetable industry some form of protection is needed against importations of this kind.
The same thing applies so far as some manufactured goods are concerned. This situation has been covered in the present Customs Act by the special value for duty provision under which, when an importation of that kind is made, the Minister of National Revenue can apply a special value for duty on the goods coming in sufficient to bring the price up to a reasonable level and thus protect the Canadian industry. Those sections of the Customs Act are being repealed by this legislation and are being replaced by a surtax in cases of this kind. The explanation given is found in the white paper at page 101 and reads as follows:
The proposed new subsections to be added to section 7 would authorize the Governor in Council to impose a surtax on imported goods that cause or threaten serious injury to Canadian producers of goods that are like or directly competitive with the imported goods. These new subsections would replace section 40A (7) of the Customs Act and in their application would have substantially the same effect as that subsection.
My hope is that the provision will have substantially the same effect as that subsection. We were assured by some of the officials that this would be the case. I would like to have a further definite assurance from the
Ways and Means
parliamentary secretary that this is indeed the case because I think it should be emphasized and publicized that this same protection will continue to exist. I would express the further hope that the application of a surtax in these circumstances will be put into effect much more quickly than has been the case in the past so far as the imposition of the special value for duty provision is concerned.
I might mention my personal experience while minister of agriculture. On quite a number of occasions I tried to have a value for duty imposed on fruits and vegetables coming into Canada. I found that it was always a slow process to obtain agreement in respect of putting the value for duty provision into effect with the result that serious injury was caused the fruit and vegetable industry while the delay was taking place. In many instances this action was not taken at all. The reason that was always given was that it might cause some form of retribution or might be interpreted as being against the provisions of GATT or something else along that line. We were assured in the committee that this situation could be improved without coming into conflict with our commitments under GATT. Therefore I repeat that I hope that once this legislation is in effect there will not be the hesitation there has been in the past in making use of this surtax on seasonal imports, imports of fruit and other imports that come into Canada at low prices and which, by and large and as a combined group, have done more damage to Canadian industry than actual dumping has done.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks this afternoon will be brief, principally because we generally agree with the position Canada and the government are taking in this regard. I must say that the way the committee operated was enough to convince anyone that all the political parties in this house can work together effectively for the improvement of legislation. I should like to pay my compliments to the hon. member for Gatineau as the chairman of the committee. He did an outstanding job. Let me compliment also the hon. member for Windsor West. Although it was sometimes difficult to know whether he was acting as a member of parliament on the committee or advising the civil service, in either capacity he did an outstanding piece of work for the committee.
I felt rather proud of our behaviour as a country in respect of the international agreement on anti-dumping. Our negotiators were

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
tough enough to protect our interests, yet at the same time they were sufficiently forwardlooking to realize the benefits that flow from honouring international commitments. The behaviour of our people and our government stands in sharp contrast to that of the United States which seemed to take a rather ambiguous position about honouring international agreements. It seems to me the United States is prepared to honour these agreements as long as they do not conflict with their laws. This hardly seems to me to be a good way to embark on an agreement upon which many countries of the world have decided. When an international agreement is arrived at it means that each of the countries involved gives up a little of its sovereignty in return for a step toward a more harmonious and logical international structure. In this regard I think Canada has behaved well. I think our negotiators did extremely well in honouring these international agreements.
There is one aspect of the anti-dumping legislation which has perhaps been wisely left very flexible. It relates to the question of injury. The debate in committee revolved around the question of what is injury and how one goes about defining it. This has been left for the determination of a board or tribunal. There is a danger that injury could be defined in a too rigid way or in such a way it could actually do more damage than good. The nature of injury will always be difficult to determine. I suspect that in the long run the question of injury will in some way have to be a political decision. Since all types of injury are incapable of one definition I do not see how those who apply the differences can do so oblivious of the economics of this country. The implication, therefore, of what I think is one of the central parts of this legislation is the fact that the government will be left on the hook. It will not be able to say, if there is dissatisfaction with the application of the legislation, that it was a civil servant or the tribunal that made the decision.
The very application of the definition means there will have to be in some related way a political implication. That is the way it should be and I am not quarrelling with this concept. I hope there will be some attention paid to the condition of the economy when a decision is handed down. Quite frankly, what may constitute injury under conditions of full employment will be different from what we may consider constitutes injury when the unemployment rate is 5 per cent or 6 per cent

as it now is. This will have to be taken into consideration.
Since the feeling of most hon. members is that Canada should move toward a world of freer trade and a less restrictive approach, an easier definition will be more acceptable when our industries are operating at capacity, when our farmers have markets and when our people have full employment, than when there is unemployment and a reduction in production. We have not heard the last of the definition of injury, and we will not with the passage of this legislation. I think this question will continue to return and we will have to consider it from time to time. We should be aware of the government's policy at any given time in relation to the concept of injury.
One of the difficulties of this legislation involves the question of proof. Of course, this created a difficulty in the previous legislation. If anything this measure is better than the previous anti-dumping law; at least, some of the industries which appeared before the committee seemed to feel we were moving in the right direction. In this regard we have to be very much aware of loopholes in terms of selling prices or costing in exporting countries. During the committee hearings I made some suggestions to departmental officials that they consider the use of a form which would put the onus of proof on the exporters rather than having our people running around trying to figure out to what extent the prices are legitimate or camouflaged. I recognize that our existing forms to some extent fulfil this purpose, but I think we could go farther than we have. I hope that the departmental officials will put their considerable talents to the task of finding a way of putting more of the onus of proof on the exporters rather than on the limited number of investigators we have at our disposal in the department.

I began my remarks by saying I was very proud of the role our people played in the negotiations respecting anti-dumping legislation. I also pointed out that perhaps others were not honouring the spirit of the negotiations as well as they might. I think it might be worth while for us to state that we are prepared to continue to be co-operative and to be internationally-minded in regard to legislation of this type but we will not tolerate being taken advantage of if other countries disregard their responsibilities. I believe

we should make it very clear that our commitments will continue to be honoured and our good faith will be displayed, but if this is not reciprocated or if attempts are made by other parties to counteract the good intentions of this legislation, we will examine our position. We should not be afraid to say this openly and boldly. We should use this as leverage to ensure that others will observe the spirit of the negotiations to the same extent that we have.
I should like to pay tribute to the members of the committee. I can say this without indirectly flattering myself because I joined the committee only in its last few weeks; I was not a member of the committee from its inception. Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks on the resolution respecting anti-dumping.
Detrimental anti-dumping duties are called for by many industrialists in our country. Anti-dumping regulations which formerly existed are no longer considered satisfactory by Canadian industrialists. In fact, we have witnessed a great deal of discrimination in the field of anti-dumping. The anti-dumping legislation is very complex, Mr. Chairman, because it is difficult to apply, enforce and control, in view of the volume of international trade of which each country wants its share. Every country has a production surplus that it cannot absorb and it tries to export more in order to get American dollars and balance its international payments. Since the American dollar has become the instrument of international trade and since it controls practically all international relationships, many countries are forced to import because they are hungry for American dollars.
As far as we are concerned, we would like very much to increase our imports because our warehouses are bursting with goods. Our
Ways and Means
industrialists would be pleased to import, but that is not always easy, because that depends on the goods we can offer. In Canada, western wheat is our most common product and the one we export on a large scale. We have a substantial surplus that we would very much like to export. But it is not always easy to export our products without accepting other products in return.
For instance, two years running Russia purchased wheat in Canada and paid for it in American dollars and gold. That enabled us to reduce our balance of payments deficit. Then, after two years, Russia asked us if we would agree to accept other goods in exchange for our wheat and I think that Canada replied that it was impossible. In view of Canada's economic situation and surpluses of products which we already had in Canada in various fields we did not agree to that deal with the Russians, and it was the same for several other countries.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
At the present time, Mr. Chairman, we know that Japan is one of the great exporting countries, that its prices are competitive and that it exports a great deal of radio and television sets. In fact, we receive in Canada a large quantity of those Japanese products which not only cost much less but which are actually quite often superior to ours as far as quality is concerned.
I shall simply give the example of Japanese television sets imported into Canada which are much cheaper than our Canadian television sets although they are of a better quality according to several technicians who do not only tell us but prove that the quality of these sets is better than that of Canadian sets. Therefore, the demand for those various sets is quite strong, because the quality is good and the price is competitive. As a matter of fact, sometimes there is a difference of about $150 between a Japanese and a Canadian T.V. set and this, after having paid the duty, transportation costs, etc. In view of those facts, Canadians demand similar prices, because it seems that this is more in line with Canadian pocket-books.
In the brief it presented to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, the Canadian Shoe Manufacturers Association mentioned the white paper on anti-dumping, and I quote:
Opinions vary widely on the merits of the new international code on the application of the antidumping duties and on the necessity of revising present anti-dumping Canadian legislation that it

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
might conform with the principles of the international code. However, Canada being one of the signatories of the "Anti-dumping code", it is obliged to respect it. We will therefore not discuss the merits of the international code.
Before discussing specific clauses of the bill, we should like to point out that the present antidumping act is less discretionary. The bill, because of the introduction of the concept of "injury" requires a high degree of administrative vigilance and a far greater use of judgment on the part of officials and members of the tribunal. The bill confers an administrative factor of capital importance.
As we have already mentioned, the former minister of finance, Hon. Mitchell Sharp, pointed out that when dumping caused or can cause injury to Canadian producers, the government intends to see to it that, in Canada, anti-dumping duties are applied properly and efficiently.
Under present legislation, there are no definite restrictions on the retroactivity of the application of anti-dumping duties. The bill proposes, under clause 5, a limited degree of retroactivity, namely 90 days, from the moment when the deputy minister makes a preliminary determination of dumping in respect of goods the shipments of which constitute massive imports or are part of a series of imports to Canada which, taken as a whole, are massive and take place over a relatively short period of time.
The new legislation will not permit only a first dumping shipment but also a series of dumping shipments which would be even more damageable. In addition, clause 5 requires that more judgment and more discretionary powers be exercised.
Mr. Chairman, the members should read carefully the following excerpt found on page 8 of the brief, and I quote:
What constitutes a massive importation?
What constitutes a relatively short period of time?
We recommend that the new anti-dumping legislation provide for the levying of anti-dumping duties in every case and in those cases where goods imported were dumped, thereby causing or being liable to cause injury to production in Canada.
With regard to the investigation procedure, the brief continues:
Clause 13 is the first to deal with investigation procedures. It states that the deputy minister shall "forthwith" cause an investigation to be initiated, on his own initiative, if he is of the opinion that there is evidence that the goods have been or are being dumped and if he is of the opinion that there is evidence or the tribunal advises that it is of the opinion that there is evidence the dumping has caused, is causing or is likely to cause material injury to the production in Canada.
It is proper to note that the requirement to act "forthwith" does not apply until the deputy minister has formed an opinion. The text does not specify that the deputy minister shall form a quick opinion.
Furthermore, there is no requirement under clause 13(4) that the deputy minister shall act promptly upon receipt of a notice from the tribunal.

It is very important for the members of the tribunal to have some experience of industry and the procedures followed before that tribunal should be quite simple, that is exempt from too many formalities.
Mr. Chairman, in this white paper there are a great many very complex formalities. I would not want to delay the passage of this resolution, but I think that, in Canada, as abroad, if the necessary purchasing power were available to buy the goods which are needed, importation would not be as necessary.
In the present world economic situation each country tries to rob the other of its markets through massive shipments of goods, which in several countries will finally bring about disorder. I would even say that importations could lead to war. All countries should imitate Canada which, in 1968, for example, produced $68 billion and exported and consumed $40 billion, leaving $28 billion worth of goods. It will be said that these products are capitalized, and it is true, because they are stored, they stay in warehouses, in the stores in view of the fact that the Canadian people do not have enough purchasing power to buy them. Each country must therefore find ways to enable the taxpayers to have the necessary purchasing power for domestically produced goods.
Consideration should have been given to another factor. Some countries have abundant primary products which they can manufacture or finish. I think some kind of planning should be established whereby one country could manufacture products which are appropriate to its basic resources, whereas production in another country should be based on its own wealth of primary products so that raw materials would be processed domestically. I would have appreciated studying this problem in the course of a committee meeting, but due to my being away for some time, 1 did not have this opportunity.
As I was saying before, as concerns antidumping, I think some means should be found other than producing and importing without taking into account markets in Canada and those that may exist in other countries. Distribution and consumption can be achieved without any large increase of production in our country, considering our natural resources, our technological progress and all the advantages in a country such as Canada. If more consumers are required, we are certainly in a position to accept more immigrants. Population can be increased. A greater number of immigrants can be welcomed,
December 17, 1988

since we need more consumers to dispose of those surpluses of commodities which are also found in each country.
There are some countries, and Canada could be one of them, which pay compensated discounts on their products in order to reduce prices and facilitate exports into other countries. I think that Canadians, at the present time, are purchasing goods which have been subsidized by foreign countries. Now, if this attitude is allowed in various countries, it should also be allowed here in Canada. We are capable, if we have surpluses, of granting a compensated discount in order to facilitate exportation of such surpluses and consumption by our own people. If the products cost too much, if our Canadians do not have the necessary purchasing power, we can surely enable them, through a compensated discount on prices, to consume more to their greater satisfaction.

I think it is somewhat of a coincidence, Mr. Chairman, that this issue comes before us in the midst of the debate on the report of the committee on procedure because sitting in the committee which considered this matter was one of the most rewarding activities in which I have participated during the short time I have been here. There was a spirit of co-operation which indicated that the committee system works. If committees are provided with the facilities for which we hope, then in the future the committee system will work extremely effectively.
As has been mentioned, there were some 22 meetings of the committee and the chairman deserves credit, as does the parliamentary secretary who guided much of the deliberations of the committee during those 22 meetings. Members from the other side of the house and from this side moved along from point to point in a spirit of co-operation. It was not a debating society; no one was trying to make points. We realized we had a job to do and we got along with it.
I think this spirit is more evident in the intimate atmosphere of a committee than in the somewhat combative atmosphere we find as we face each other across the bastions of this house. I might say that we got to know one another, perhaps not to the extent we would have liked. I am afraid we did tend to sit on opposite sides of the table, but perhaps as we get to know one another better even
Ways and Means
that tendency will disappear. It was very important, since we are in the midst of a rules debate, to see and experience a committee working well. Men from all parts of the country were gaining a perspective that is only possible when they meet men from other parts of the country. This was indeed an enlightening experience for everyone who participated in the deliberations of the committee.
The committee went beyond a mere examination of the anti-dumping provisions and the white paper. As a result members gained a very excellent insight into Canadian industry as a whole. Though we perhaps strayed too frequently from the direct purposes of the committee, I believe, we all benefited from the education we received. As one industry after another presented us with completely different problems, we learned something about those industries which will help the members of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs to function a great deal more effectively and intelligently in the future.
Perhaps one of the most interesting experiences, one of the most exciting things for all Canadians, occurred on the day we listened to the brief from the steel industry of Canada. This industry does have its dumping problems and those problems have to be looked into. However, it is an interesting industry. The rates of pay are as high as those in virtually any industry in Canada and, what is equally important, they match or exceed those paid in the same industry in the United States. The industry is highly profitable in that it generates a great deal of new investment in new plant, new technology, and so on. They have reached a technological level that is second to none in the world, and as well the industry pays its shareholders good dividends. As far as I can recall, this was the only industry that was wholly Canadian owned. It is free to move without checking with anybody else anywhere.
Sometimes there was a tendency on the part of the members of the committee and those appearing before the committee to fail to differentiate between tariffs and what is legitimate dumping. As they become more familiar with this new anti-dumping legislation I think that the people in industry, the producers, will be able to make this differentiation.
The question of injury was critical in the examination of this legislation. Injury can be very difficult to prove, and many hours and

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
many meetings were spent on this issue. The interesting part was that everybody seemed to accept the fact that broad discretionary powers were needed. The legislation provides for the establishment of a panel which will have this discretionary freedom. Thus we can implement this measure in the proper spirit of the Kennedy round negotiations. We heard words and saw words in brief after brief to the effect that this must be done forthwith, expeditiously, immediately and precisely. There was a great deal of concern about this.
I can understand the apprehension that prevailed because a year or so ago I sat on the opposite side of the table during the negotiation of the Kennedy round machinery tariff. This industry, with which I was associated, had these same apprehensions. However, there is something new and exciting as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations. There is a spirit abroad which I feel has permeated the departments concerned, particularly the Department of National Revenue, and as a result there is a desire to make this plan work. The new machinery tariff has been in effect for almost a year and there has not been a single complaint during that time. This is very encouraging. I believe that the anti-dumping provisions will be implemented in the same spirit, in a highly intelligent and imaginative way.
We forget that these negotiations are a twoway street; the arrangements are reciprocal. Additional opportunities are provided to us for the protection of Canadian exporters. The spirit of the Kennedy round which is abroad will enable us to function effectively in the international trade arena. There are dangers if we sit back and try to hide behind our tariffs or what is left of our tariffs. We will be given a challenge, an opportunity to get into other markets abroad and show the entrepreneurship which is so essential to this country and from which our industry will benefit greatly.
I have not spoken for 20 minutes. I have only spoken for about 7 minutes, I think, but I have nothing more to say so I see no reason to speak for 20 minutes. I think we should bear this in mind during the rules debate as well.

First, Mr. Chairman, I would like to compliment the government on the way it has handled this proposed legislation. Ten, 15 or 20 years ago the party in power, regardless of which one it was, would have introduced such legislation and said to the manufacturers of Canada, "Here it is; take it or leave it." But that is not so this time. The manufacturers or their associations had ample opportunity to appear before the standing committee and present their briefs, ideas and suggestions, and the members of the committee were willing to hear them. Furthermore, the committee made amendments which I understand have been almost 100 per cent accepted. So I compliment the government on its approach to this legislation. But in case members of the government might become too elated over what I have just said, I would like to remind them that the late C. D. Howe did not bend over backwards and think too favourably of Canada as an exporting country. He seemed to feel that we would not stand much of a chance as an exporting country.
However, in December, 1960, the then minister of trade and commerce, the hon. George Hees, introduced the brilliant idea of assembling our trade commissioners from all
Ways and Means
over the world in Ottawa and inviting Canadian manufacturers to meet with them, thus putting across the idea that if Canadian manufacturers were given an equal chance they had a wonderful opportunity to export their goods. He aroused their imagination and since that time Canadian manufacturers have realized they have an opportunity to become large exporters. Give Canadian manufacturers a fair break, give them an opportunity to play in the same ball diamond with the same set of rules and I am convinced they can compete any place throughout the world. So I am glad to see this anti-dumping legislation brought forward to give them some protection.
This anti-dumping legislation gives to the Department of National Bevenue, which will administer it, more discretionary powers than have ever been given to any department of government. We, as parliamentarians, have grave reservations about discretionary powers. It is a subject which has been debated at great length in this chamber. The standing committee felt that in order to administer this legislation discretionary powers had to be given to that department, but now that we are giving the department those powers we expect it to act quickly and to be vigorous and prompt in administering the legislation. If the officials do not do that, then the legislation is of no use. It is useless unless those administering it take hold of it, give it a new approach and bring in new people who have the ability to administer the legislation as it should be administered. I am not suggesting that they go out and build a great empire to do this. I think they already have the men in the department. It will be a matter of reorganizing the department for the application of this anti-dumping legislation.
Above all, the administrative staff will require expert chartered accountants, men who can go into the English market, the Italian market, into manufacturing plants abroad, look at their books, study their costing methods, and be able to say whether those manufacturers have arrived at the right, proper and normal value. If we send a man who does not understand his work, who is not a specialist in accounting, he will be lost and will not be able to establish the normal value for export purposes.
Great power is also given to the deputy minister, and he will have to work quickly. The legislation says he must "forthwith" do this and do that. Forthwith does not mean a week from today. It is now, and the standing

December 17, 1968
Ways and Means
committee was given to understand that that is just what is meant.
Sometimes it is difficult to get information from boards and commissions such as the hydro-electric power commissions of the various provinces and the Canadian National Railways. Sometimes they refuse to give the prices at which a tender is let. How can one establish the normal value if one cannot find out all the information? I am glad to note that the draft bill contains in clause 11 this provision:
Where, in the opinion of the deputy minister, sufficient information has not been furnished or is not available to enable the determination of normal value or export price under section 9 or 10, the normal value or export price, as the case may be, shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes.
This means that if they do not want to give this information the department has the power to demand it, and I sincerely hope it will use that power in securing all the information required.
A tribunal is to be established consisting of five men. Who will these men be? Will they be capable men? Will they be men who have great experience in commerce and industry or will they be political appointees? If they are appointed on a political basis and not on the basis of ability the tribunal will be useless and the act will not be administered as it should be. When the government picks these five men who will make up the tribunal-and it is the tribunal whose word is final on whether or not a dumping duty should be imposed-I hope it will pick men well experienced in commerce and industry. I also hope the tribunal will report its findings promptly.
The draft bill also contains a clause dealing with the terms and regulations of the tribunal. I hope we will be told who will examine these regulations or terms. Will they be cleared by parliament or by the cabinet? I am not too sure on that point.
I am also a little concerned about a situation which could very well happen in Canada. I think all hon. members are aware that many American corporations operate branches in Canada. Let us assume that a United States corporation, with a subsidiary in Canada which has 90 per cent, 95 per cent, or even more of the Canadian market in respect of one product, has branches all over the world. It is possible it might decide it could make the product it is making in Canada more cheaply at one of its foreign plants. So it would decide to manufacture this product

at another plant elsewhere in the world. Thus the Canadian plant would be closed down and many people would be out of work. Who would complain that there was dumping? It is certain that the corporate company in Canada would not complain because it would bring the product in and no dumping could be charged against it. It could continue to bring it in and no one would register a complaint. The only safety valve in this regard, and the one on which we would have to depend, would be that the union in that plant, if it felt that an injury had been caused it, would be perfectly within its rights to register a complaint with the tribunal and say that injury had been caused because the employees had been put out of work. I feel that this anti-dumping legislation is a step in the right direction. After all, our regulations have not been changed to any great degree since 1904. It is time this was done.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I sincerely hope that all the other countries which are involved in this agreement will carry their weight. It has not yet been proven to me that the United States will decide to go ahead with such legislation. I presume this will be the case, but I think Canada should know this first before it moves too fast so that we will begin anti-dumping legislation on an equal basis. Anti-dumping legislation is not the over-all answer. It is not the answer to help Canadian industry to survive. It certainly is a help but it will not correct the situation altogether. We must look at the existing non-tariff barriers and do something about them in the form of legislation. Nothing in this legislation will relieve the problem of low wage countries exporting to Canada in great quantities.
I am told that Italy, with a wage rate about one-third that in Canada, is a large manufacturer of electrical appliances. Italy will and is now exporting these products to Canada. They have other advantages, including a tax structure which the Canadian manufacturer does not have. While the Canadian manufacturer has a 50 per cent corporate income tax slapped on his profits a company in Italy may only have to pay 5 per cent in income tax and in addition is allowed to plow all its profits back into development and research. These are the type of things that are causing real problems in Canada.
Then we have the most-favoured-nation agreements. We have such an arrangement with Russia which I think expires next year. Because of this agreement heavy dump trucks
December 17, 1968

and power shovels that are made in my riding must compete with the heavy equipment brought in from Russia because Russia was given most-favoured-nation treatment. I pause to wonder why this concession was given. When it comes up for renewal I hope the house will give very serious consideration to the facts behind it.
We also have a treaty with Australia. Australia exports canned peaches to Canada. This is causing problems for the Canadian fruit growers.
A free trade agreement in respect of agricultural machinery was made in 1944. It was a one-sided agreement. No mention was made of parts. Now we have the situation of Canadian agricultural machinery manufacturers deciding to move their plants to the United States. The Canadian plants that were supplying parts for agricultural machinery are now trying to export the parts to these plants in the United States. They find there is a duty on Canadian agricultural machinery parts and therefore they cannot send these parts into the United States without paying a duty while the United States manufacturer of agricultural parts can ship these parts into Canada duty free. I wonder what goes on here. These non-tariff barriers are certainly detrimental to the manufacturer in Canada.
Then we find that the government gives business to offshore companies. This is another thing which we should take a look at. I know for a fact that transformers used on the Nelson river project here in Canada were supplied under a contract given to the U.K. Electric Company in the United Kingdom. When that tender was given this Government knew that Canadian industries are not even allowed to quote a price in the United Kingdom. Yet we turn around and give the U.K. Electric Company an $8 million contract to supply the transformers for the Nelson river project. Because of this 1,000 men have lost work for a period of a year in my riding since the General Electric Company did not receive the contract for those transformers, and they were the second low bidder. I must not enlarge on this any more, but I did want to mention that the non-tariff barriers are just as important and perhaps more so than the anti-dumping legislation. However, the anti-dumping legislation is a step in the right direction.
I shall conclude by saying what I said at the beginning. Give the Canadian manufacturers the same set of rules. Let them play on anywhere in the world.

Your committee wishes to underline the necessity of prompt and effective action to ensure the carrying out of the intent of proposed legislation with regard to injurious dumping.
For this reason, Mr. Chairman, the composition of the anti-dumping tribunal is a very important matter. Again the committee commented on this in its report when it said:
Your committee recommends that the tribunal be duly constituted with members of the highest calibre at the earliest possible date.

I would therefore urge upon the government that it obtain as wide representation as possible on the tribunal when it is appointed.
During the committee hearings it was noted there were some difficulties in respect of the interpretation of the code and the application of it in dealing with less than arm's length transactions of United States subsidiary firms operating in Canada. negotiations it was felt that Canada's position with regard to anti-dumping legislation, that is, the power of the deputy minister of national revenue under section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act, was a form of discrimination and was, shall we say, one of the non-tariff barrier practices. Under our economic system, the sole objective of trade consists in realizing more and more profits at the expense of others. This financial system automatically results in lack of purchasing power on the part of the consumers. Therefore, it is clear that this legislation will afford some protection to the Canadian producers wanting to monopolize the domestic market.
Besides, Mr. Chairman, on reading the evidence gathered by the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, as well as the various briefs submitted to this committee by producers, associations and groups, it can be realized that they are interested solely in protecting their customers through Canadian legislation preventing imports of foreign products that would take a larger share of the Canadian market.
Arguments put forward are indeed very persuasive. For instance, it is argued that imported products at lower prices than other similar products manufactured in Canada will jeopardize the Canadian industries, reduce the number of jobs and perhaps cause the bankruptcy of several industries. Some emphasize that it is essential for Canada to be protected against foreign exports as our trade balance with other countries may be seriously affected.
We, of the Ralliement Creditiste, do not accept these arguments because we believe in an economic system geared to the satisfaction of human requirements and to the subordination of the methods to the results we are proposing. Consequently, as we have always

Ways and Means
indicated, we are guided by the following principles.
The purpose of economic order is to ensure that the needs of the consumers are met, and nothing else.
The end is more important than the means, and the means must be subordinated to the end, and the hierarchy of the various ends must be respected.
The purpose of industry, in all its forms, is to supply goods and services, and not employment. Industrial organization is that much more perfect when it produces more while requiring less human work, leaving man free to exercise his activity in humanizing works.
Money has no other purpose than to help economic life to achieve its end without obstructing it, managing it, or conditioning it.
The nature of things, sane reason and social justice teach us that the end of economic activity should be none other than the material prosperity of society, the well-being of the whole human community. The economy must not aim towards creating wealth for its own sake, or for only a few and it must endeavour to satisfy the needs of all and to produce goods which really make richer all citizens of the country.
In economics it would be said even more plainly that the end of the economic activity is to serve the consumer first. That objective must inspire any truly social, truly human economic policy.
The aim of the economic activity is to meet the needs of the consumers. However, the needs of the consumers will be met more easily and more fully if the products they need and want to get are available to them at prices they can afford.
It can be said that the legislation under consideration affects the consumers very closely because it can deprive them of the products they could not get at the prices now in force in our economic system.
International trade is made essentially of commercial transactions between countries. Purchases of shirts from Hong Kong, shoes from Italy, wines from France, woollens from Great Britain, these are imports for Canadians, imports of goods which other countries can offer to Canadian consumers at better prices, or goods which are not produced in Canada, or which are difficult to produce here according to recognized standards.
Conversely, sales of news-print to the United States, of wheat to Soviet Union, of bacon to Great Britain, are exports for

Canada, exports designed to meet the needs of the consumers in those countries.
Thus, it can be said that international trade is a sound thing, and so we must support any measure designed to abolish hindrances, to enable consumers to satisfy their needs. In fact, if some countries produce easily and abundantly certain goods, other goods are better and more plentifully produced elsewhere. So trade between consumers of different countries is a beneficial thing.
However, we must realize that one of the greatest difficulties in international trade stems from the fact that countries want to export more than they import, to ensure a "favourable trade balance".
In fact, we know with what insistence public relations men in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce make every effort to show us that we export more goods and services than we import.
This philosophy, which is not that of the Social Credit, is based on the principle that gold and silver alone are desirable. If such tenets were justified, all trade between countries and even between citizens in a country should be abolished.
Assuming that gold and money were the only wealth, we could brand as madmen people who would be giving away their money to buy a suit or a car. However, today everyone realizes-and consumers are no exception -that what they need is bread, food and clothes, which are the true wealth and which will fill their every need.

The purpose of the bill is to permit the British Northwestern Insurance Company to change its name to Eagle Star Insurance Company of Canada, and to increase the authorized capital. Although fully owned by the British company, Eagle Star Insurance Company, all but two of the directors of the Canadian company are Canadians. I point this out merely because some hon. members in previous debates raised objections. Despite the objections of some hon. members to the fact that this company is owned by a British parent, I point out that this bill asks for no substantial changes in the company. As I said, the company invests in Canada and most of its directors and personnel are Canadians. The hon. member for Kent-Essex was kind enough to note that I come from the same area of the country as he does, and that I share his concern about some of the matters he mentioned. I certainly share the concern of all hon. members from the area with respect to the interests of the area's agriculture and industry, a concern shared for example by my colleagues, the hon. member for Kent-Essex and the hon. member for Windsor-Walker-ville.
Perhaps I should note, with reference to some of the very interesting comments made by the hon. member for Kent-Essex, in particular with reference to the corn situation which was very disturbing to many, that the action taken by the government with respect to corn imports was actually taken not under the existing provisions with respect to dumping but under the present value for duty section of section 40 (a) which is being replaced by the section 7 to which I have just made reference.
Often people refer to action of this type as being dumping action. If I am not mistaken, the term "dumping" has a rather precise meaning in the law of international trade, in referring to sale in one country at a price
Anti-Dumping Duties
lower than the price at which the same goods are sold in the country of export, and it is not intended to apply to the problem of low cost imports when the goods are sold at what is considered to be a rather low price in relation to domestic goods but not at a price lower than they are sold in the country of export. It is with respect to the latter situation that action under the existing value for duty section was taken, and it is with respect to these value for duty sections that the government is proposing that they be replaced by a new section 7 which will make somewhat clearer that this type of action is emergency action authorized by section 19 of the GATT, and is not really meant to be included in legislation dealing with dumping. This is one reason why the existing section is being replaced with another one. The purpose is to make more clear the nature of the action that is intended to be taken with respect to low cost imports of the type which cause injury to Canadian production.
I might also say with respect to the comments of the hon. member for Kent-Essex, when he expressed some concern about the time that will be taken under the proposed new legislation with respect to dumping, that perhaps he may be reassured if he notes that the proposed legislation imposed time limits within which action must be taken, time limits which do not exist under the existing law.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary also expressed concern about the problem of low cost imports of agricultural products. He had something to say about the trade agreement with Australia. I am informed that this agreement does not exempt imports from Australia from the application of our dumping law, but rather it creates an obligation to consult with the Australian authorities when a complaint of dumping is made either with respect to goods that are intended to be imported into Canada from Australia or with respect to goods that are intended to be imported from Canada to Australia. But again, as I understand it, the agreement states that the consultations must be completed within a certain time period. If mutual agreement is not reached within that time period, then action under the dumping legislation can be taken. As I say, this is a reciprocal provision which would apply also if complaints are made with respect to the export of goods from Canada to Australia.

Anti-dumping legislation should be regarded as an extension into the international field of principles expressed nationally by statutes restricting discriminatory or predatory trade practices. Dumping is an unfair trade practice, and I wish to emphasize this point to the parliamentary secretary. It is a lessening of free competition, and sometimes it destroys free competition. Besides being unlawful, dumping in the long run is contrary to the public's interest. The result	is that
although politically we are no longer a colony, we have been subjected to economic exploitation in a manner that few other countries have experienced.
Last	summer	we	witnessed	wholesale
dumping of agricultural products, corn, poultry and others, from the United States, with no action by the government. In textiles we have been subjected to subsidized dumping from the United States and Japan. In footwear we have been subjected to dumping from all over the world. The result is that Canadian industries have gone out of business and we have become a nation importing finished products while forcing more and more of our enterprise into primary industry. No nation can go on doing this for very long.
We have been in the position of living off our principal, and using our resources to buy the things we need, rather than manufacturing those things here in Canada at a cheaper

price. Resources do not last forever and in a few years Canada, instead of being a resource rich nation, will be a resource poor nation in many fields. The point I wish to make is that continued toleration of large scale dumping of surplus industrial and manufactured products, as well as agricultural products, will make future generations of Canadians hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Canada has been in the position of an open city, or open country. We have practised the open door policy in so far as foreign goods are concerned. A few years ago we made some effort, by arriving at mutual understandings with countries such as Japan and the United States, to limit the amount of foreign dumping in order that native Canadian industries would not be smothered under an avalanche of cheap goods coming in from other countries. Now with the Kennedy round agreements, the situation is likely to be worse than ever.
This anti-dumping measure is a reluctant recognition by the government that some action must be taken to protect Canadian industry. It is interesting that this measure should be brought in by a party which over the years has proclaimed itself all out for free trade. But nevertheless one cannot help wondering how much protection is afforded the Canadian producer by this bill. As I have said before, it does not go far enough. It is simply paying lip service to the need of preventing Canadian industry from being overrun by dumping from abroad.
The record of the government in international affairs is not reassuring. The Liberal party has a long record of placing international relations above the interests of the Canadian producer. We know how the Kennedy round discussions became an instrument for delaying the signing of a new grains agreement and how Canadian wheat producers suffered by being undercut in the interim. We have been told that Canadian industry will not suffer. Obviously this clause is an attempt to lock the garage door after the automobile has been stolen-and an American automobile at that, Mr. Chairman.
What we now have, obviously, is a tribunal, a sort of court of last resort to which the Canadian producer, when he is on the verge of bankruptcy as a result of having his market undercut, can appeal for some kind of action. Knowing how most of these tribunals work, it is highly unlikely that action will be forthcoming before the producer is compelled to close his doors.

There is another point that must be made in connection with this whole question. It is not merely anti-dumping legislation that is required. There are many cases of Canadian products being designed, developed and manufactured in Canada, and even a market created for them in Canada and sometimes the United States, and then American corporations with their superior financing, large run economies and larger markets at home have moved deliberately into the market created by a Canadian firm and, over a period of time, have simply collared that market for themselves. This is not an exception, Mr. Chairman; it is almost the rule.
This is not done by dumping within the terms of this legislation. It is done simply by making use of the economies of production available to American producers in the American market. The dumping comes later when the Canadian product has been eliminated. At that point the American manufacturer can simply dump his surplus product in Canada, taking over the market created in Canada by a Canadian producer whom the American has either bought out or pushed out. I fail to see any way in which this clause protects Canadian producers against this kind of monopolistic competition. Yet in my opinion this is the most common kind of unfair competition facing Canadian manufacturers of finished articles, the competition from gigantic American competitors who move in, once a Canadian firm has created a market and, either through the parent U.S. corporation or through setting up a Canadian subsidiary, simply take over the market.
Anti-dumping provisions therefore do not prevent the cannibalization of Canadian industry by gigantic American or other foreign competitors, for the simple reason that under the unrealistic definition of dumping there is no dumping until or unless: "the normal value of the goods exceeds the export price." Under the definition of normal value it is only considered to be dumping when a product is sold in Canada at a price lower than the price at which it is sold in the United States. But, Mr. Chairman, it can be just as harmful to Canadian industry when the product is sold at the same price as the price at which it is sold in the United States, because very often the greater volume of American production permits huge economies in production. But that situation is not taken into account in this bill, so far as I can see.
The fact that the goods must be sold below the domestic price in the Canadian market
Anti-Dumping Duties
means that a great number of goods which can be sold cheaply and made cheaply in United States or Japan can come into Canada. This applies to Czechoslovakia, East Germany and other European and Iron Curtain countries which can send their products here at exactly the same price at which they are sold in those countries and, because of currency differences and production economies, undercut Canadian manufacturers to a considerable degree.
This is why I said this bill does not answer to any great degree the problem of Canadian manufacturers being undercut by unfair competition from other countries. They would not fall under the dumping definition. This is where the clause falls short. Within a short time the government will be facing a serious situation in the form of complaints from producers all over Canada.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I shall give just one other example, Mr. Chairman, and I do not know whether it has been touched on or not. As we know, our seasons in the north range from winter into the spring, and then into summer, so that quite often goods on sale in the country to the south of us have reached their peak market before they come into the Canadian market. Therefore the producers of those goods can afford to sell them here below their actual cost. They can lower their prices because they have already sold 75 per cent, 80 per cent or 90 per cent of their production. Not only that, but the output of one U.S. firm on occasion equals the total production of all Canadian manufacturers of a particular article. One can cite instances where one big corporation in the United States can manufacture more goods and dump more into Canada than the total annual production of Canadian manufacturers. This is of great concern to me. Once those are in the suppliers' hands how can this law be enforced? Therefore, that is the reason I do not think this bill and this clause will accomplish what they are intended to accomplish.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words on the anti-dumping legislation. The objectives of the bill are certainly to encourage Canadian manufacturers and to protect them against the entry into Canada of goods similar to those manufactured in Canada but at much lower prices.
However, this bill, which is intended to protect Canadian manufacturers, says nothing

December 17, 1968
Anti-Dumping Duties
about consumers and their needs in view of the present economic situation of Canadian or foreign manufacturers.
Anti-dumping is being practised not only between the Japanese and the Americans or other countries in the world, but even within our own country, between one town and another, for example. Obvious examples of this are to be found in the trade between Ottawa and Hull, two adjoining towns which are practically one. However, Ottawa people buy in Hull and Hull people buy in Ottawa because of tax differences between Quebec and Ontario; that constitutes dumping. In fact, Hull people come to buy in Ottawa because prices are lower. The consumer cannot be blamed for seeking lower prices. If, for example, a consumer can buy rubber shoes made in Japan at half the price of the corresponding Canadian-made product, one cannot blame him.
Instead of passing anti-dumping legislation designed to keep prices high, the government should introduce a bill to subsidize Canadian industry, in order to compete with the prices of goods dumped by other countries on the Canadian market and to protect the Canadian consumer. This is not what we are doing. Dumping is not practised only in Canada, because we do it ourselves in other countries.
For instance, Mr. Chairman, it is impossible to find out how much we are paid for the wheat we are selling to Red China. This is then a case of dumping when subsidies cover about one half the normal price of wheat. We are selling our wheat to China at a much lower price than production cost. This is dumping practised by Canada towards other countries.
At one time, we were blaming the United States for selling their wheat to Russia at better prices than ours. American economists and the American government were asked to keep in line with our prices.
The problem will remain the same, Mr. Chairman. This will not increase the purchasing power of our consumers by one red cent. Even with the adoption of this bill, our people will not be in a position to buy more. Perhaps some products will not be admitted to Canada or the government will be able to levy import duties so that these products will reach approximately the price levels of Canadian products, but the purchasing power will not in turn be stimulated; the reverse will be true. I think this is a direct infringement-

Here is the situation, Mr. Chairman. We are selling our wheat to China at less than prime cost, than cost price, and it is impossible to find out from the minister what prices we are being paid for the wheat we sell to China.
