That is what happened not so long ago-in fact barely three years ago-but I hold my ground and I maintain that we are selling our wheat to the Chinese or the Russians for less than it is costing us to grow it here. Each time we traded with those countries we had to sell our products at lower prices and that represents Canadian dumping in those foreign countries to which we sell wheat.
Mr. Chairman, I am not against our selling wheat and our being competitive but I object to our selling our products below cost because we have a surplus. However, Canada acts towards the other countries as they do towards us. That is what I mean when I say that this will not help the consumer. It may help the producer, true. It may please the manufacturers of textile products, of rubber, or any other goods.
We want to protect our industry and I suggest this way of doing it. Instead of dumping in other countries, let us give our Canadian manufacturers subsidies to enable them to

reduce their prices and sell their goods to the Canadian consumers.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Then production would achieve its end which is to meet the needs of the consumer. That is the solution of the Ralliement credi-tiste. It is not a far-fetched solution because any intelligent person can understand it.
On the one hand, we dub as unfriendly those countries which sell their goods at extremely low prices; on the other hand, we try to export our goods to those same countries.
We want to help the Canadian people, not only the manufacturer. Canadian manufacturers export and receive subsidies to do so. If it can be done for exports, why can it not be done for consumption here in Canada? Would it be asking for the moon? These subsidies would allow prices to be lowered, and this, in turn, would increase the purchasing power of consumers. It is as simple as that.
However, instead of looking at the economic situation from the point of view of the consumers or of their interests, the government is only concerned about the production angle. Mr. Chairman, the problem is not one of production, but of prices. Actually, production is very healthy. It can be doubled or tripled so long as there is a corresponding demand. The real problem is one of distribution and of consumption of goods manufactured in Canada and outside the country.
We will always have to deal with other countries. We will have to exchange Canadian wood, for fruit from Florida, for example, or wheat against Chinese products. Transactions will always have to continue and even improve.
However, that must always be done in the interests of the consumers and not only for the pleasure of enriching a few persons, such as importers or exporters, and still less financiers who strangle the working people, the farmer as well as the worker. We are not at all interested in protecting and enriching those people. Those who will read Hansard to-morrow, will know that the Ralliement Creditiste is not interested in those who want to make profits out of anti-dumping laws, but in protecting the Canadian citizen.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the few remarks that I wanted to make tonight. The government owes it to the Canadian people to consider the consumption aspect of our economy and our transactions with other countries. Let us grant to our Canadian people the same
Anti-Dumping Duties
subsidies which we give other countries so that they may come and buy here. Instead of taxing and over-taxing the Canadian people in all sorts of ways, let us help them, and the problem will be solved.
We can effectively lower the cost of consumption or production through subsidies; then, we shall become better competitors in the international market and we shall be able to face dumping, as we call it. There would be no need to pass anti-dumping legislation if we were to guarantee every Canadian citizen a purchasing power which would make it possible for him to purchase Japanese, Chinese or Canadian products. In fact, this is the only way we can protect our Canadian industry by granting subsidies so that our people may face international competition.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to rise a short while ago to ask some questions of the responsible minister. Now I am on my feet I would also like to refer to some remarks made by the previous speaker, whom I hope I understood correctly. With regard to dumping wheat in China or any other market, this charge should not be brought, and if it is brought, it cannot be substantiated. The wheat that Canadians sell overseas through the Canadian Wheat Board is sold at international prices, without the benefit of subsidy, and I would like to quote some figures to substantiate my point. I am sorry I am speaking only from memory in this regard, but in the area of Vulcan, Alberta, the figure arrived at as the result of a cost study was $1.70, or $1.76 a bushel. This is the cost of production in that area of Alberta, which is one of our good wheat producing areas, comparable to some of the better areas in Saskatchewan or Manitoba in what might be called the dry country.
If you take the export figure at which wheat has been sold, ranging from $1.96 to $2.12, and the difference in the cost of transportation, and so on, you will find it compares with that figure. I would not like the committee to be under the impression that this is a subsidized price for exports. It is not. If you take the cost of transportation and the cost of marketing, you will find that at this figure you are coming very close to the Vulcan figure of cost production.
As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has just said to me, the figures I am quoting are for grades 1, 2 and 3 wheat. If it happens to be low grade wheat, you will be very much in the hole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that was the impression I intended to convey. The proposed anti-dumping law does not make any distinction with respect to the type of goods which can create the complaint of dumping. Rather it would fall under the heading, shall I say, of low cost imports causing injury to Canadian production, because it cannot be demonstrated that these agricultural products are being sold in Canada at a price lower than they are available for sale in the country of export. Therefore a different legislative provision has to be made use of, and the legislative provision in the proposed bill, if it is adopted by this house as I hope it will be, calls for the application of a surtax. The proposed section is based on article 19 of the GATT which contemplates this type of problem facing the various trading nations.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the idea of this bill is a very good one, but I am a little afraid that we may go on a kind of witch hunting expedition here which may hurt many of our industries, if we pursue this along the wrong lines. I suggest that in order that this legislation be effective there must be a close liaison among the different departments of the government. What is good for the agricultural industry may backfire in other industries, or even in different regional parts of Canada. For instance, if we decide arbitrarily that the selling of U.S. corn in eastern Canada should be stopped, we have to be careful that reciprocal action is not taken by the United States, which will cut down on the importation of coarse grains and fodder from Canada into the northwestern United States.
We are living in times of change. At one time perhaps it was safe to generalize and to say that western Canada was a free trade area. This may well be so when we are trying to sell our wheat, but when we are confronted with the problem of selling our oil, particularly in Alberta and now in the Arctic, we are up against a different thing. Free trade in oil would ruin the oil industry of Alberta at the present time. Before we suggest that the United States is dumping Venezuelan oil in Canada, we have to remember that we have to protect our large oil market in the northwestern United States. At the present time we have a gentleman's agreement with the United States according to which they will sell Venezuelan oil in Montreal, and we will be able to ship our oil through our pipe lines into Seattle.
So we have to be careful that we are neither regional nor blind in this matter. As I said, a closer liaison will be necessary among the agriculture, industry, trade and commerce and the revenue departments to make sure that what we mean to do does not backfire. I think that the stress should be put on reciprocal agreements, and perhaps we should use this legislation very sparingly and only use it as a final stick. But if we plan properly and if we ensure a closer liaison between the different departments, I do not think that this dumping legislation will have to be put into effect very often. As has been pointed out by

If we had a proper world grain agreement, and if we had solidified Canada's trading position in this field, then I do not believe we would have to worry so much about the dumping of corn in eastern Canada or about not having any sales for fodder and coarse grains from western Canada. We should have a viable economy which would draw together all of our industries, agriculture, our manufacturing industry and primary producing industries such as oil.
What I would envisage would be this: If we are going to be faced with the dumping of oil on our Canadian market, I think the people from our industry could build a pipe line system across Canada so that our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce would be able to forestall the dumping of United States oil on our markets. They would be able to offer United States interests cheap Canadian facilities, and we would at least then have our fair share of oil moving through this pipe line. This is the kind of planning we need. As I say, I feel this is a necessary piece of legislation but it should only be a stop-gap; it should only be emergency legislation. We should forestall any need for invoking this measure by careful planning and by good reciprocal agreements, particularly with the United States which is our greatest competitor in the manufacturing field, in the oil field and in some cases even in agriculture.
Let us not forget that the United States is also our best customer in all these fields. We are only now becoming an aggressive young manufacturing nation. However, we still have a tremendous stake in agriculture. Western Canada has perhaps a half agricultural and half industrial economy, but the agricultural half still has to be protected. I do not want to see Canada going off half-cocked barring corn entering Ontario, because then the United States could say, "All right, no more beef can be shipped into Montana and no more hay into the Dakotas in the dry season."
I should like to see a great deal more liaison between our government departments, so that by careful planning and co-operation with our own primary producers or through making reciprocal agreements, particularly with the United States, we could forestall the

need for dumping legislation. We are in a good bargaining position. The United States wants our friendship and co-operation and in some cases they want our cheap oil, our better beef and our competitive grain. However, we have to be willing to make reasonable concessions in return.
If we planned our turkey imports on a quota basis, there would be no need to flood our markets at Thanksgiving or Christmas with cheap turkeys from the United States. This ruins our small producers. As one or two other members have said, it is too late to lock the door after the horse is out of the barn. After our turkey producers have been put out of business, then United States producers are in a position to recoup all their so-called losses by jacking up the prices, in co-operation with the chain stores. In this way they recover the money they were presumably risking by giving us cheap turkeys for one year. We find ourselves in a position where our own producers are out of business, and we have to pay the price.

There is the determination whether the normal price is higher than the export price, and therefore whether there is a margin of dumping. Second, there is the question whether this dumping is causing injury to Canadian production.
It is the job of the tribunal to make a determination on the question of injury. I take it then that the government feels there can be dumping without injury.

INDIAN AFFAIRS-COMPETITION FOR POSITION AS ADVISER ON POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight because I wish to speak on a question that was ruled to be inappropriate about a week ago. Over a century ago the Indian affairs department started out to administer treaties and to protect rights of native peoples, but according to Indian leaders, because of its paternalistic attitude it has gradually over the years become the oppressor rather than the protector of the very people it was developed to assist. It is perhaps fair to say that no other department of government enjoys so little confidence among the people it is structured to help. There is little real dialogue between the department and the native people themselves, in spite of repeated proposals from the natives that they take part in the decisions which affect them.
The record in respect of the treatment of Indians during the past 100 years in appalling. I could document this if I had time. Despite the expansion of the department by 10 per cent from 1966 to 1968 this expansion has resulted in little observable improvement in the services that will enable the Indians


and Eskimos to improve their ability to function in society with independence and dignity. As little as 5 or 6 per cent of the total budget of the department for salaries is being spent on employees of Indian and Eskimo origin. I should like it to be noted that the term "persons of Indian and Eskimo origin" is a very vague one. This does not mean that the money is being spent, in spite of the pitiful 5 or 6 per cent, on wages and salaries for reserve Indians. Metis or off reserve Indians are not covered under the act, but they are of Indian and Eskimo origin.
I think the main problem in the department is that the bulk of the budget is being paid to too many white chiefs, and that not enough trickles down to the Indians. To support this I should like to read from page 385 of the Senate Debates for the year 1968:
The Department has 927 senior officer positions of which 801 are presently occupied. Of these, 17 persons are of Indian and Eskimo origin. Sixteen of the 17 persons are all occupied with Indian Affairs and represent 4.4 per cent of the senior positions occupied. A number of the 801 senior positions are concerned with education supervision.
Need I say more? If we take out the school principals and supervisors, this 4.4 per cent figure shrinks alarmingly. It is then accurate to say that the major decisions affecting native people are made by men, dedicated as they may be, who are in no position to understand Indian aspirations, because they are not Indians themselves. The door is barred to Indians in this department having a real voice for a long time to come. This brings me to the central point of the question I asked in the house:
Has the Indian Affairs Branch recently advertised a competition at the PM6 level with a salary of $18,000 to consult with the Indian and Eskimo people on policies and programs affecting them? This competition, as I understand it, is not open to qualified native applicants.
Upon investigation I learned that the position was not really a competition at all but an internal promotion-some would say a political promotion within the department itself- with the incidental right of appeal by a native applicant within the department, if he felt he could meet whatever criteria might be set for the position. I think it is important that people know how these appointments work. First, they are not open competitions designed to secure the best man available from throughout the land. They are, instead, advertised narrowly within the department, and I imagine those in the know realize very early upon whose shoulders the magic wand has been placed.
December 17, 1968	COMMONS
The executive committee, which really means the deputy minister, chooses a person to fill the position. The right of appeal exists, of course, for any other employee if he is brave enough to appeal the choice, in this particular case before the expiry date of December 18. That is tomorrow, Mr. Speaker. Can you imagine who in his right mind would risk making an appeal in such a patriarchal system, if he wanted to get ahead?
The particular position in question is for the chief of the Indian-Eskimo bureau in Ottawa, a very important position in light of the growing desire of native Indians and Eskimos for a greater voice in their affairs and decisions affecting them. I think this position requires a man of considerable experience in dealing with the problems of native people. If not a native himself, he should have the respect of the people with whom he is to deal. He should possess a real empathy for native people. He should like them and be liked by them, because the position requires that the successful applicant cooperate with native people and enjoy their confidence in order to facilitate communication and learn with them.
What is the history of the applicant designated to fill this very important and sensitive office? My information is that there is little in the applicant's background which would qualify him as chief of the Indian-Eskimo branch. I apologize to the minister and to the applicant in advance, if my information is either unfair or inaccurate. The designated man is a former serviceman, an ex-air force officer. He was formerly employed in public relations in the office of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) when he was minister of national defence. He later worked in public relations for the centennial commission, or was at least under contract to and employed by the centennial commission. Over the past year, and for one year only, the applicant was employed as executive assistant to Mr. R. F. Battle, assistant deputy minister of Indian affairs. He came into Indian affairs without competition. As far as I know he has never been before any civil service board. Now he is slated, after one year's experience in Indian affairs, to be moved from a $13,000 to an $18,000 per year position, without competition.
Two weeks ago in Ottawa the founding meeting of the National Indian Brotherhood took place. Indian leaders from all across Canada are demanding a greater voice. This kind of staffing and promotion practice within

Mr. Speaker, how can the Indian leaders believe that the department of Indian affairs is sincere in its desire for better relationships when a public relations man of one years's experience in Indian affairs can be promoted to a position of such importance without competition? Public appreciation of Indian problems and public sympathy and support for a better break for native people is in my view at an all-time high. Practices such as I have described only lower the image and prestige of the department of Indian affairs and, indeed, government generally. In my view it is about time we began to set our house in order in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, on December 13 I asked the Minister of Transport if he would abandon the proposal to enlarge the Toronto international airport at Malton. In the few minutes allowed me I shall try to persuade him to do so.
During the last three months I have done a great deal of research on the subject. My views have been fortified by studies conducted by the municipalities and by others. In addition, I have received objections, with reasons, from thousands of families who would be adversely affected.
I have concluded that the proposal is holding up the production of 19,000 housing units


or accommodation for 50,000 people in Mississauga and Etobicoke. Living conditions would become unbearable for another 50,000 people now living to the south of the proposed enlargement. It would impair or destroy housing accommodation for another 150,000 people living to the east. Dozens of schools and hospitals would have to be soundproofed at great cost, and even then their efficiency would be lessened. It would disrupt the planned course of development, and thus the economic stability of the municipalities concerned. It would withdraw about 2,000 acres from a limited supply of 40,000 to 50,000 acres of land ready for urbanization, and thus have an extreme adverse effect on housing and other urban developments in the Toronto metro area. It would conflict with the Ontario planning act and be an insult to the planning of the area, as planned by the municipalities and approved by the province and by the Department of Transport itself. It would commit the federal government to pollution, in the sense that where investment is large enough we must accept it and thus make it impossible ever to cleanse thoroughly the air in the Toronto area.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Think of the air in ten years, at a time when there is no wind and thus no movement of air, with 2,000 flights a day spewing gas and carbon over the area. I understand that each plane burns approximately four tons of fuel during a take-off. This could lead to a total of 10,000 tons a day in the 1980's. Future generations would rightly condemn us.
The proposal has been rejected by all of the municipalities concerned. Their refusal to rezone the land for flight paths means that such land would have to be purchased, and the cost of the land alone would, I believe, be at least half a billion, whereas the original estimate for the whole project was approximately $300 million. Appropriately, the Central Ontario Planning Institute of Canada concluded that the expansion is wrong and would lead to a growing and insoluble conflict between the metro demand for land and the airport's demand for control.
A more acceptable and less expensive site can and must be found. I suggest for consideration a site on undeveloped and inexpensive land north of Kingston for a double jet port to serve Toronto and Montreal. If this is thought to be too far into the future, then perhaps Camp Borden would provide a site, since the government already owns 20,000
December 17, 1968	COMMONS
acres there. In both cases, the land is submarginal farm land, and could be acquired at a minimum cost. The recent trend in North America is for jet ports to be 50 to 100 miles from city centres. Pending development of rapid transit, there could be flying bus service from smaller ports such as de Havilland and the island in Toronto, by means of the new short take-off planes.
A second alternative, that of a floating airport seems worthy of investigation since the flightways would be over open water and would disturb no one. Leading civil engineers hesitate to estimate the cost, but feel a study costing about $100,000 would be a worthwhile investment. In fact, the United States federal aviation administration has just recently launched an intensive study of this solution. Two immediate objections, those of water pollution and a greater use of United States air space for descending planes, are not really tenable.
The airport of the late 70's or early 80's will require a staff of perhaps 30,000 people with a supporting city having a total population of perhaps 200,000. Rather than cause these people to settle in Toronto and Montreal metropolitan areas, where land is scarce and at a premium, we should plan for a new city to be compatible with an airport which would help to relieve the pressure in the metro areas, and at the same time allow the development of a new city on a pre-planned and logical basis.
Since severe intensification of flights would be as undesirable as the major expansion, I support a second airport as early as possible, but better still now, sufficiently removed to avoid a repetition of the present problem, and where land is inexpensive and can be zoned to provide for future further expansion.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO PRICE OF TOYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Prime Minister the following question on orders of the day:
In the absence of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I wish to direct my question to the Prime Minister. In view of the outrageous prices being charged for Christmas toys this season, would the Prime Minister consider requesting the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to conduct an immediate investigation into this serious problem?
In a supplementary question I noted that millions of dollars are spent on toys, that there are only a few shopping days until Christmas and that advertising creates additional pressures on our society. My interest in this question was aroused on Saturday when I accompanied my wife on a Christmas shopping expedition. We were appalled at the prices. Since our oldest child is now over eight years of age we have had some years of experience in Christmas shopping for our own children, within the limitations of a family budget. On this basis we noted that prices had skyrocketed since last year.
We were interested in buying several items in which our children had expressed interest, largely as a result of viewing television advertising. The items in which we were interested ranged from $15 to $30 or more, each. This was beyond the family budget. After our initial shock we started to look around. There was hardly any toy selling for less than $8 which would give any child pleasure. Curiously, there were a number of items which had been marked down to half price. I suggest that very likely these were not loss leaders, because they were still selling at a considerable price. Rather, they represented items where the desired profit had been made on the total consignment of the item, and the remaining stock was being sold at a lower level of return.
A friend who heard of my inquiry sent me the following note:
I bought Billy Blastoff for $8.88 at a well known toy store. I've since seen it for sale in other stores
December 17, 1968
4088	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion at several different prices, including as low as $4.88. This price range seems ridiculous. We parents need protection.
On Monday, prior to orders of the day, I purchased a plastic building set for $8.98, plus tax, and presented it to the Prime Minister following my question. I hope he enjoys playing with the set and that it will give him some relief from the tensions of office. I believe I obtained the beginner's set; with it I hope the Prime Minister may make more progress than he has so far in building his just society. Possibly he is fortunate that I did not give him the instant insanity set of blocks.
Since then I have discussed this matter with other people. I heard of one case where a four year old girl decided she wanted a particular make of doll. When her mother took her to see Santa Claus at a store the girl informed him she wanted the doll and Santa replied, "You tell your mother we have your doll already wrapped for you." On investigating the mother found the doll cost over $18, and had considerable difficulty, of course, in persuading her daughter that it would be better to buy another doll.
Another mother here in Ottawa investigated the toy situation just after Christmas a year or more ago. She was informed by the merchandising people that any toy could be sold through television advertising. They also told her that toys advertised on television could be sold for three times the ordinary retail price.
Christmas giving is a tradition in our society, stemming from the giving of gifts to the child Jesus in Bethlehem. Down through the centuries the giving of gifts, particularly to children, has become a tradition. Foisted on this beautiful tradition is the influence of mass advertising, and particularly television. The crass commercialization of Christmas for purposes of profit has prostituted this tradition. The conventions of our own society help to create a captive market in the Christmas season. The impact of television advertising constitutes a form of torture, used to squeeze out every possible dollar from the consumer under the guise of Christmas tradition.
I witnessed the impact of television advertising just this evening. My wife and I were looking at a Christmas catalogue and noted a "happy, happy doll" selling for around $15. Our four year old son was able to recite the words of the television ad at the mere mention of the name-"She laughs, and she'll make you laugh, too". Millions of dollars are


spent on toys each year, and toys bring merchants one of the highest levels of retail mark-up. I am reliably informed that the average retail mark-up on toys is well above 40 per cent. I am also reliably informed that the retail price of toys is generally double what they cost to manufacture.
Further questions of toy safety have arisen. In the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, December 13 we read:
So you're thinking of buying your daughter a miniature vacuum cleaner or sewing machine just like mommy's for Christmas?
Better think again. Consumers Union in the United States tested 42 electric toys of this nature for last months' issue of their magazine Consumer Reports, and found ten to be unacceptable from a safety standpoint.
The article goes on to give many examples. This is an excellent illustration of the type of thing that should be tackled by the Department of Consumer Affairs. Only a few shopping days remain until Christmas. If the Department of Consumer Affairs is to be effective it must develop a capacity to cope with such situations as this in a matter of a few days. Only in this way will the new department be of real value.
In the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, December 14, appeared an article under the heading: Space toys "in", guns "out". In it we read:
Canadians are spending more than ever in the frantic crush of pre-Christmas buying and toy-makers forecast sales about 30 per cent higher than last season.
The '67 seasonal sale totalled about $180,000,000, or $32 per child.
I am sure this is a matter worthy of investigation by the department.

I listened intently to what the hon. member said as to the price of toys, particularly since during the Christmas season all citizens with families of young children have the purchase
December 17. 1968	COMMONS
of toys very much on their minds. In attempting to ascertain the degree to which the current price of toys is a matter of concern to consumers we have checked returns to box 99 which, as hon. members are aware, is the facility through which the consumers of Canada register their complaints with the department. I find there has been little reaction to the price of toys. Out of fewer than 3,000 complaints since the inception of box 99, only 23 have related to toys and of these only two were concerned with price. There is, of course, a wide selection of toys available on the market, presenting the consumer with the opportunity to make a choice as to the variety, quality and, above all, price, to suit his purse. speechtext:
Letter from Mr. Fowler to Mr. Benson Dear Minister Benson:
In completing the 1969 United States balance of payments program and while arranging for an orderly transition, I thought it would be useful to review the unique financial relationship which exists between our two countries. This was last described in the exchange of letters I had on March 7, 1968, with your predecessor, Mitchell Sharp. In my letter I noted: "Unique financial relations between our two countries have been a mutual support to both and to the international monetary system. These relations have served the interests of both our countries without interfering with the domestic policies of either." Events since March add a new endorsement to this judgment.
This unique relationship which our two countries share is a natural reflection of a common and peaceful border of some 5,500 miles. It reflects as well the importance of trade and capital and neighbours who move across this invisible boundary. Recognizing this interdependence, we have long since believed that it is not in the interest of either country to occasion destabilizing influences on our currencies which might inhibit the other country in the pursuit of its own economic objectives. To this end, our policies in this field have been to support our overall objectives to our mutual advantage.
This is the reason, notwithstanding the crisis then raging in the gold markets of the world and only shortly after the President's New Year's day balance of payments measure, that in March we were able to exempt Canada from our balance of payments measures. This exemption and your reaction to it was indeed "mutual support." Canada was thus assured of access to our markets for a wide range of capital transactions, enabling Canada to continue its traditional method of financing its current account deficit with the United States and permitting financial institutions in both countries to operate flexibly.
This latest recognition of the interrelationship of our international payments is also the reason you have taken constructive actions to ensure that Canada is not used as a "passthrough" channel by which the purpose of the
United States balance of payments program might be frustrated. Moreover, the policy under which you invest your foreign exchange holdings is to our mutual advantage.
This is also the reason that in the exchange of letters last March we reiterated the basic principle that it would not be Canada's intention to increase its foreign exchange reserves through borrowings in the United States. Implementation of this principle does not require that Canada's reserve level be limited to any particular figure. We are well aware of Canada's need for flexibility with respect to reserve levels in order to accommodate the adaptation of monetary policy to the changing needs of its domestic economy, seasonal factors and other influences of a temporary nature. This statement of objectives recognizes that under circumstances in which an improvement in the payments position of the United States is essential to the strengthening of the world monetary system, it is in Canada's own interest to avoid hindering the achievement of this objective by unnecessary borrowing in the United States. In recent times capital markets in other countries have developed a capacity which has attracted borrowers from many countries. Canadian authorities have taken advantage of these expanding capital markets to raise funds in substantial quantities. These developments now offer Canada an alternative means of achieving an increase in its reserves whenever Canadian authorities believe this is desirable. In addition, Canada has given strong support to the arrangements for new special drawing rights which, when activated, will offer a source of regular and automatic additions to international reserves. Both our countries, along with other nations, actively support the ratification of this new facility in the International Monetary Fund and the activation of these reserve assets as soon as possible.
In undertaking this review of our relationship, I have been very much aided by the knowledge and experience our respective governments have gained through the close consultations which form such an important part of this relationship. These consultations will, of course, continue to permit us to keep each other fully informed of our views regarding current financial developments.
December 17, 1968

The unique financial arrangements we have developed, expressed first with the joint statement of July 21, 1963 and brought up to date today, provide support to the payments positions of both countries and hence strengthen the international monetary system.
Sincerely yours, Henry H. Fowler.
Letter from Mr. Benson to Mr. Fowler
Dear Secretary Fowler:
I welcome the review of financial relationships between Canada and the United States which you have provided in your letter of today's date.
As you have noted, the Canadian government is keenly aware of the importance to Canada and to the world, as well as to the United States, of the strength of the United States dollar and, as a means to that end, of a continued improvement in the international payments position of the United States.
With this in mind, the Canadian government has adopted policies to ensure that the exemption of Canada from the United States balance of payments program would not endanger the success of that program. In particular, we have taken steps to prevent Canada from becoming a "pass-through" channel for the flow of capital from the United States. We have also found various appropriate means of supporting the payments position of the United States. Thus the Canadian government has invested its United States dollar reserves (in excess of working balances) in special non-marketable issues of the United States treasury. It also turned to the expanding capital markets of Europe to
find funds with which to rebuild Canada's foreign exchange reserves. In the course of this year substantial sums have been added to our reserves as a result of borrowings of the government of Canada and other Canadians outside the United States, and the investment of these sums has provided support to the payments position of the United States. We expect, as you note in your letter, that the implementation of the special drawing rights scheme in the International Monetary Fund will provide an additional well-regulated source of new reserve assets.
I too have found very useful the close consultations which have come to form such an important aspect of the relationship between our two countries. I look forward to a continuation of them as a means of keeping each other fully informed of our views regarding current financial developments.
In the light of all these considerations I can reiterate to you that it is not an objective of Canadian policy to achieve permanent increases in our exchange reserves through unnecessary borrowing in the United States. I fully share the view expressed in your letter that the implementation of this principle does not require that Canada's reserve level be limited to any particular figure, and that our reserves may be expected to fluctuate to accommodate the adaptation of monetary policy to the changing needs of the domestic economy, seasonal influence, and other influences of a temporary nature.
Yours sincerely,
E. J. Benson,
Minister of Finance.
Wednesday, December 18, 1968
